newsitem.title: USA: N.J. state senator wins Democrat nod for governor.
newsitem.headline: N.J. state senator wins Democrat nod for governor.

text.p: State Sen. James McGreevey, running as a traditional Democrat emphasizing education, narrowly won Tuesday's New Jersey Democratic primary for governor.

McGreevey's victory over U.S. Rep. Rob Andrews and former Morris County prosecutor Michael Murphy sets the stage for a general election challenge in November against Republican incumbent Gov. Christine Whitman.

Whitman, a star of national Republican politics who remains well-liked at home, is strongly favored to win. But analysts have said her reelection is not guaranteed, due to dissatisfaction among some voters over her economic policies.
"Governor Whitman can, should and will be defeated in November," McGreevey said in a victory speech after Andrews conceded defeat and offered his support.

With 99 percent of precincts reporting, McGreevey had a 7,278 vote margin with 39 percent of the vote, against 37 percent for Andrews and 21 percent for Murphy, who ran an unexpectedly strong campaign casting himself an outsider unbeholden to state party bosses. A fourth candidate, Frank Marmo, had 2 percent.
McGreevey, who also is mayor of Woodbridge, N.J., had campaigned on a theme of state support for "lifetime learning" and drew on the support of labor unions and county party organizations.
He criticized Whitman in his victory speech for property-tax and car-insurance rates he said were too high and for conducting what he called a "government by gimmick."
McGreevey was known for supporting a 1990 tax increase that led to Whitman's 1993 election ouster of Democrat Gov. Jim Florio, but then voting for most of Whitman's proposed tax cuts.

Andrews had earned a reputation as an advocate of tax and spending restraint in Congress. But he sought in his campaign to moderate that image, which had drawn attacks by McGreevey for being too close to the House Republican leadership.
Murphy claimed a moral victory in defeat. "A new day has dawned in New Jersey politics...the organization doesn't control everything," he told supporters.

Analysts have said Whitman may be vulnerable due to voter dissatisfaction over local property tax hikes in the wake of the 30 percent income-tax cut that has been a hallmark of her administration, and over a lack of action to combat high automobile insurance rates.
Whitman outlined themes of her re-election campaign at a rally of her own Tuesday night.

"We're running on a record that's put New Jersey on a road to a better and brighter future," Whitman said. "New Jersey has been a model for cutting taxes, reforming welfare (and) passing tough laws on crime."
A Mason-Dixon poll last week for News 12 New Jersey television gave Whitman a 52 to 33 percent lead over McGreevey among registered New Jersey voters. A total of 800 voters were surveyed.
